text: Every SIEM vendor sells some version of SOAR, and the pitch often implies the platform decides what to do about an alert the way a senior analyst would. That's not what's actually running under the hood. This lesson pulls the acronym apart into its three real jobs, so you know exactly what you're building in this chapter, and exactly where its limits are before you wire anything together.

Orchestration is the wiring — getting Sentinel, your ticketing system, identity, and EDR to pass data to each other through one workflow instead of an analyst tabbing between five consoles. Automation is running a fixed, repeatable sequence every time a condition is met — deterministic, not judgment-based. Response is the one piece that actually changes state in the real world, and it's the piece this chapter treats most carefully.

A Logic App playbook can't weigh conflicting signals, like an unusual sign-in location against an open change-ticket for planned maintenance, unless you built a check for exactly that case. It can't judge whether a specific action is proportionate right now. And it has no model of a novel situation — every action it takes was anticipated in advance by whoever built it, which is exactly why containment gets an approval gate later in this chapter.

In Microsoft Sentinel, the practical SOAR stack is two pieces: an Automation Rule that watches for incidents matching a condition and decides what to trigger, and a Logic App playbook that's the actual workflow of connector actions — enrichment, orchestration, and anything gated behind human approval. Neither piece makes a judgment call on its own; both just execute exactly what you configured them to do.

By the end of this chapter you'll have a real Automation Rule and playbook that enriches an incident with real context before anyone looks at it, and prepares — but never unilaterally executes — any containment action with real blast radius. Next, you'll build the rule and playbook itself.
